text: What does the name Satan mean? Hey everybody, I'm Dan Mlelen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and religion. And the name Satan comes from the Hebrew word satan,
which can be a verb or a noun. But in the Hebrew Bible, it is never used as a personal name. It's used to refer to
someone who is acting hostile to another or is acting as an adversary. So it can mean to be adversarial or to be hostile
or it can be a generic noun that means an adversary. And so in much of the usage it is used in reference to human
beings who are being hostile or adversarial to one another. And then in some instances it refers to other divine
beings. For instance in numbers 22 the angel of the Lord who confronts Balum
does so as a satan. And then in some usage and particularly later usage around the Persian period you have it
used with the definite article Hatan the adversary. And this is not yet a personal name. It seems to be a title
for a specific role or position within the divine council within the hierarchy of the heavens. And so in Job 1 and 2,
you have Hassatan, the Satan who is among the Benet Elohim when they come to present themselves before the divine
throne. And in Zechariah 3, you also have Hassatan. And the closest thing we have to the word Satan maybe being used
as a personal name is in 1 Chronicles 21:1 where Satan is the one who incites
David to conduct a census so he can tell if he has enough fighting men in order to go up to battle. And this is considered inappropriate because David
is supposed to put his trust in Adonai who is going to fight his battles for him. And this is parallel to 2 Samuel
24:1 where it's actually God themselves who is the one who incites David to conduct a census. So what we might have
on the part of the editors of 1 Chronicles 21 is replacing God with Satan. Now it could just be an
adversary, an unnamed adversary who is inciting David as a replacement for God's incitement of David. But some
scholars argue that this is actually the first occurrence of the use of Satan as a personal name. I don't think that is very likely, but that is a common
argument. Now, it's within second temple period Judaism where you begin to see Satan used more regularly as a title for

different names. They're called Shmeihaza and Asael and Azazelle and Miraasha and Mastema. And there are four
occurrences of the word Satan in the book of Enoch. Two of them are singular and two of them are plural. So Satan seems to be a class of deity. You have
references to the Satans. But then you have the titular use, the use of Satan as a as a title, as a role in reference to this head malevolent angel as well.
And then when we get to the Septuagent,
the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, Satan sometimes, and particularly when it's in reference to a
divine being is translated as the avalos, which is transliterated into English as devil. So the word devil in
Greek, which means something like slanderer, is the closest equivalent that they could get to the Hebrew Satan,
accuser or adversary. And it's not until the New Testament that we finally see Satan or Satan being used as the
personal name of the head malevolent divine being or entity who is in charge
of all the demonic forces and who is the enemy of God. So, the name Satan actually originates around the time of
the New Testament. Prior to that, it's used either as a generic noun, a way to refer to an adversary or someone who is
being hostile, or it's a role within the divine council. But either way, the name comes from a word that means to be an adversary or to be hostile to others.
